terms: what is snap called in vermont
supplements.citation: Vermont DCF 3SquaresVT consumer page (dcf.vermont.gov); myBenefits portal; Code of Vermont Rules 13-170-005
supplements.heading: Vermont's public brand is "3SquaresVT" — a distinctive state name, unlike Delaware's plain "SNAP" — and it covers the full federal SNAP program administered by DCF's Economic Services Division
supplements.text: Vermont's Agency of Human Services, Department for Children and Families (DCF), administers SNAP under the state-specific public brand name "3SquaresVT" across all of DCF's own live consumer materials, its legislative testimony, and its application forms (Form 202, or Form 202-3SNP for the simplified age-60+/disability process) — a genuinely distinctive state nickname in the same family as California's "CalFresh" or Washington's "Basic Food," and unlike this roster's Delaware pack, which found no distinctive Delaware-specific nickname at all. Vermont's Code of Vermont Rules citation itself is titled "13-170-005 - FOOD STAMPS (3SQUARESVT) (270 TO 280)" — the older federal "Food Stamps" name and the state brand name appear together in the regulation's own title, an intentional pairing rather than an unamended artifact (contrast this roster's Delaware pack, which found an unintentional naming mismatch between different sections of its own manual). Vermont's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DCF's ESD — a state-administered program with no county-level policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Delaware, Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, and New Hampshire packs. Vermont's current self-service application portal is myBenefits (also used for Reach Up, Essential Person, and Fuel Assistance); applicants can also apply with a paper Form 202, submitted via ESD's secure document uploader, by mail, or dropped off at a district office.

supplements.citation: Vermont DCF 3SquaresVT Income Guidelines page (published October 2025); Vermont DCF 3SquaresVT consumer page; Restaurant Meals Program Implementation Analysis (2/19/2025)
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: Vermont runs TWO distinct categorical-eligibility routes — the standard 185% FPL BBCE gross-income gate AND a separate, state-specific route for households with children who received the Vermont Earned Income Tax Credit — either one clears the resource test entirely
supplements.text: Vermont DCF's own current 3SquaresVT Income Guidelines table (published October 2025) shows two dollar columns by household size: an Expanded Gross Monthly Income limit at 185% of the Federal Poverty Level ($2,413 for household size 1, $4,957 for size 4, +$848 per additional member) and a Maximum Net Monthly Income limit at 100% FPL ($1,305 for size 1, $2,680 for size 4, +$459 per additional member) that a household must also clear to receive a monthly payment. Per DCF's own main 3SquaresVT consumer page, a household is categorically eligible — meaning it does not have to pass either the gross or net income test — through either of TWO distinct routes this pack confirmed independently: (1) gross household income at or below 185% FPL (the standard BBCE mechanism most secondary sources describe), OR (2) the household has children AND received the Vermont Earned Income Tax Credit within the 12 months before applying, a state-EITC-linked categorical-eligibility mechanism this pack found is DISTINCT from route (1) and is not merely a restatement of the same 185% FPL test — structurally the same BBCE-family mechanism this roster's Delaware pack found (there, triggered by a TANF-funded pregnancy-prevention-information service), but implemented through Vermont's own state EITC program rather than TANF. This pack flags, as it did for Delaware, that this is a genuinely more precise structure than a flat 'no asset limit in Vermont' claim: a household that clears NEITHER route (for example, exceeding 185% FPL gross income with no EITC-linked child in the household) can still qualify only if it includes a member 60+ or disabled, in which case DCF's page states the household's resources (savings, property, excluding the home and certain retirement accounts) are then considered, with a resource limit of $4,500 for that narrower elderly/disabled non-categorical track — this figure matches the current federal FY2026 COLA-adjusted resource-limit ceiling under 7 CFR 273.8(a) exactly, in contrast to this roster's Delaware pack, which found its own regulatory text citing a stale, below-federal-floor $2,000/$3,000 figure. This pack also caught and corrects one small secondary-source dollar-figure error: a secondary aggregator (snapbenefitcalculator.com) states the household-size-1 gross income limit as approximately $2,461, while DCF's own current published October 2025 table states $2,413 — a real, if modest, discrepancy this pack resolves in DCF's own published figure's favor.

supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP FINDING (primary-source statutory confirmation): Vermont FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban by statute in 2009 — one of the earlier and cleanest full opt-outs among the states in this roster
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack fetched Vermont's own statute directly and confirms Vermont's opt-out is complete, simple, and long-standing: 33 V.S.A. § 1203a states in full, 'An individual domiciled in Vermont shall be exempt from the disqualification provided for in 21 U.S.C. § 862a,' added by 2009 No. 1 (Sp. Sess.), § E.323.2 — meaning Vermont has had a full, unconditional drug-felony SNAP opt-out on the books since 2009, notably earlier than this roster's Delaware pack, which found Delaware's own opt-out (via repeal of DSSM 2027) only took effect in 2018. This pack found this figure independently corroborated by a secondary source (the Collateral Consequences Resource Center's 50-state drug-felony survey), which categorizes Vermont as 'Fully Opted Out' for both SNAP and TANF — a case where a minority-position claim (most secondary sources this pack found for other states describe partial or conditional bans; a clean, unconditional, one-sentence full opt-out is the less common pattern) is independently confirmed by both the primary statutory text and a specialized secondary source, rather than resting on either alone. Vermont's 3SquaresVT application forms this pack reviewed (via the Form 202 family) ask about felony-related conduct connected to SNAP fraud itself (trading benefits for drugs, buying/selling benefits, duplicate-benefit fraud) — not about prior drug possession or distribution convictions unrelated to the program, consistent with the statute's blanket exemption.

supplements.citation: Vermont DCF Understanding 3SquaresVT Work Rules page; Vermont DCF '3SquaresVT Program Changes' slide deck (10/30/2025); USDA FNS ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY2025-2029 index (no Vermont entry)
supplements.heading: Vermont currently has NO ABAWD waiver anywhere in the state at all — not even a lapsed one — and its own live materials confirm the current post-OBBBA 18-64 age range, narrower child exemption, and new tribal-member exemption
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. This pack fetched Vermont DCF's own live Understanding 3SquaresVT Work Rules page directly and confirms it distinguishes a broader 'general work requirement' (ages 16-64, per the main 3SquaresVT page's own wording) from the narrower 'time limited benefits work requirement' (the ABAWD rule specifically, for people 18-64 without kids under 14 who are able to work). DCF's own dated 10/30/2025 legislative slide deck independently confirms, effective 7/4/2025 and implemented 10/1/2025 per the federal H.R.1/OBBBA law: the age range subject to time-limited work requirements expanded from 18-54 to 18-64; the child-in-home exemption narrowed from under-18 to under-14; the homeless, veteran, and aged-out-of-foster-care exemptions were removed entirely; and a new exemption was added for Indians, Urban Indians, California Indians, and others eligible for Indian Health Services — this pack found this figure independently CROSS-CONFIRMED by two of DCF's own separate primary materials (the live consumer page and the dated legislative slide deck), a stronger evidentiary basis than this roster's Delaware pack had for the equivalent finding. This pack also checked USDA FNS's own ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY2025-2029 index directly and found NO Vermont entry anywhere — not even a lapsed one, in contrast to this roster's Delaware, New Hampshire, and Maine packs, each of which found at least one past Vermont-adjacent-state waiver-response entry. This pack's reading: Vermont currently enforces the ABAWD time limit statewide with no waived area, corroborated by WebSearch describing Vermont as having had no active ABAWD waiver as of FY2024 Q4 and as not being among the small group of states (Minnesota, Montana, North Dakota) carrying an active statewide waiver through mid-2026. Separately, DCF's own slide deck discloses a genuinely Vermont-specific, time-limited event: the federal government shutdown caused FNS to pause new benefit issuance nationwide in November 2025, and Vermont's own Eboard/Administration responded by state-funding the first 15 days of eligible households' November benefits (expected issuance around 11/7/2025) plus $250,000 to the Vermont Foodbank — a more concrete, dated state-specific response than this roster's Delaware pack found for the same national event.

supplements.citation: Vermont DCF '3SquaresVT Program Changes' slide deck (10/30/2025)
supplements.heading: Vermont's current utility-allowance dollar figures ARE confirmed and dated — a contrast with this roster's Delaware pack, which could not locate its own state's specific figures
supplements.text: Vermont DCF's own dated 10/30/2025 legislative slide deck, presented by ESD's Deputy Commissioner and Food and Nutrition Program Director directly to the Vermont Legislature, states three current utility-allowance tiers effective 10/1/2025 (FFY2026) for households WITHOUT a senior or disabled member: a Standard Utility Allowance (SUA) of $1,096/month for households paying heating or cooling costs; a Basic Utility Allowance (BUA) of $311/month for households not paying for heating/cooling but responsible for two or more of: electricity, cooking fuel, water/sewage, garbage, or telephone; and a Telephone-only allowance of $37/month for households whose sole utility expense is a phone. The same slide deck confirms a genuinely consequential OBBBA-era policy change effective 7/4/2025, implemented 10/1/2025: the 'heat and eat' provision (which previously let ANY household receiving as little as a token LIHEAP energy-assistance payment automatically qualify for the highest SUA tier) is now LIMITED to households with an elderly or disabled member only — non-elderly/disabled households are instead assigned whichever utility-allowance tier actually matches the specific utility costs they are responsible for. This pack flags this as a genuine, dated confirmation rather than a disclosed gap, a contrast with this roster's Delaware pack, which could not locate Delaware's own specific FFY2026 SUA dollar figures at all. This pack could NOT independently verify these three dollar figures against a second, fully-independent primary source (e.g., a formally-published DCF COLA notice separate from this slide deck) — the slide deck itself is DCF's own dated, named, official legislative testimony, which this pack treats as reliable primary-source authority, but flags the single-document sourcing explicitly in freshness.json.

supplements.citation: Vermont DCF 'Restaurant Meals Program Implementation Analysis' legislative report (2/19/2025); Vermont DCF 3SquaresVT consumer page
supplements.heading: SECOND FLAGSHIP FINDING: Vermont has NO formal Restaurant Meals Program, but is one of only five states nationally with a SNAP cash-out option, and 43% of Vermont's entire 3SquaresVT caseload already receives benefits as unrestricted cash usable at any restaurant
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT. This pack fetched DCF's own dated 2/19/2025 legislative report directly and confirms Vermont currently operates NO RMP: DCF opposed 2024's S.215 (which would have required implementation), citing the cost of a new full-time staff position (~$125,082/year) plus EBT-vendor programming costs (~$105,192 one-time, $682.40/month ongoing). But this pack found and confirms a genuinely distinctive structural fact that several flat 'Vermont has no restaurant option' secondary-source summaries omit entirely: Vermont is one of only FIVE states nationally with the authority to issue SNAP benefits as unrestricted CASH (not EBT) to households where every member is 65+ and/or receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) — narrower eligibility than RMP's own 60+/homeless-inclusive criteria, but functionally more powerful, since cash-out benefits can be spent ANYWHERE, including restaurants, exactly like ordinary income, with no restaurant-approval or concessional-pricing process required at all. Per DCF's own report, 43% of Vermont's entire 3SquaresVT caseload — 16,823 of 39,112 households — currently receives benefits this way (deposited to checking/savings, sent as a paper check, or loaded to an EBT card as withdrawable cash, per household choice), while DCF's main consumer page separately confirms that anyone UNDER 65 gets an ordinary EBT card instead. This pack's reading: describing Vermont as simply 'no restaurant meals program' is technically true for the formal RMP option but meaningfully incomplete — a large minority of Vermont's SNAP households already have a functionally broader restaurant/hot-food purchasing option than RMP itself would provide, through a completely separate mechanism. DCF's report also notes an estimated ~2,600 homeless households and ~2,575 age-60-64 households NOT covered by cash-out (and would benefit from a hypothetical future RMP) — the population gap that a formal RMP would specifically close.

supplements.citation: Vermont DCF 3SquaresVT in a SNAP! page; Vermont DCF 3SquaresVT consumer page
supplements.heading: Vermont's standard SNAP certification period is 12 months (interim report due in month 5), extending to a genuinely long 24-36 months — up to a full 3 years with no additional paperwork — for the age-60+/disability simplified track
supplements.text: For most 3SquaresVT households, DCF assigns a standard 12-month certification period, with an interim report (Form 202IR) due around month 5 asking whether anything has changed since the household applied — a somewhat shorter interim-report timing than this roster's Delaware pack found (Delaware's interim report is due in month 6 of its own 12-month standard period). Vermont's '3SquaresVT in a SNAP!' simplified process, available when everyone applying is 60+ or receiving disability benefits, earns no job/self-employment income, and buys/prepares food together, extends this dramatically: DCF's own page states plainly, 'You'll get to keep your benefits for three years with no additional paperwork' — a full 36-month certification period with NO interim report at all, notably longer than this roster's Delaware pack's own 24-month elderly/disabled maximum, and longer than the 12-month norm most of this roster's other states use. Roughly six weeks before a household's certification period ends, DCF automatically mails a new application, and ESD contacts the household for an interview once the completed recertification application is submitted.
